newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines seeks to export sugar to ease glut.
newsitem.headline: Philippines seeks to export sugar to ease glut.

text.p: The Philippines plans to export sugar to ease a glut, a senior official said on Wednesday, but millers said they expect imports to continue because of cheaper prices overseas.

"We are not re-emerging as a sugar exporter in the world market. It is a way of saving us from this very critical condition of high inventories," Sugar Regulatory Administration (SRA) chief Wilson Gamboa told Reuters in an interview.

The Philippines, once a major sugar exporter with overseas sales peaking at 2.0 million tonnes in the 1976/1977 crop year (September-August), is now a sugar importer due to rising population and demand.
But stocks have been high this year because of imports of about 1.2 million tonnes of sugar from Australia, Thailand and Brazil between September 1995 and July 1996, traders have said.
Gamboa also said Philippine raw sugar output is expected to reach 1.9 million to 2.0 million tonnes in the 1996/1997 crop year against the previous year's 1.79 million tonnes.
"I expect production this year to equal demand," he said, adding that exports were needed to reduce stockpiles.
Gamboa said the export plans would be finalised at a meeting on Thursday of a committee set up by President Fidel Ramos to resolve the crisis.

Gamboa said that at least 200,000 tonnes of sugar needed to be exported to effectively reduce stocks and added the government has asked the United States if it could advance shipment of its remaining sugar quota.
The Philippines is a beneficiary of a programme under which the United States pays premium prices for sugar imports from developing countries.
Gamboa said the Philippines has so far exported 78,000 tonnes of sugar to the United States out of a quota of 219,000 tonnes for the 1996-1997 crop year.
However, the plan is unlikely to restrict traders from importing even more sugar, because international prices are lower than domestic prices despite steep import tariffs, millers said.
Imports are taxed at 100 percent, with a rebate of 35 percent for neighbouring Southeast Asian countries. Ramos increased the import tax from 50 percent several months ago.
But the Philippines is set to cut the sugar tariff to 80 percent starting July 1, 1997, as part of its commitment to the General Agreements on Tariffs and Trade, local millers said.
Other countries in the region like Thailand and Indonesia have committed to slash their tariffs only by 2002, they added.

"The Philippines is the only country in the world that gives tariff discounts to the importation of refined sugar," said Jose Maria Zabaleta, executive director of the Philippine Sugar Millers Association, on the rebate in import tariffs offered to other nations in the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN).
"We are asking President Ramos to withdraw the tariff discount to ASEAN countries to save the local sugar industry," Zabaleta said.
